newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rise after weak data ease rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rise after weak data ease rate hike fears.

text.p: Stocks rose in volatile trading Friday as a report pointing to tame inflation calmed investor worries about interest rates and helped erase some of Thursday's big losses.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 56.57 points to 6,935.46, recouping about a third of Thursday' 160-point drop sparked by strong February retail sales data that rekindled fears of inflation and higher interest rates.
The Dow's gains for the day trimmed its loss for the week to 65.43 points.
In the broader market, gainers outpaced losers by 1,408 to 1,028 on volume of 486.9 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The recovery began as early news of a surprisingly big drop in wholesale prices in February helped eased concerns that the Federal Reserve would raise rates in a bid to ward off inflation.

The Producer Price Index fell 0.4 percent in February, a bigger drop than economists had forecast, and the core rate excluding volatile food and energy prices fell 0.1 percent, instead of rising 0.1 percent as expected.
The report cast doubt on forecasts that the Fed, the nation's central bank, will raise rates at its policy-making meeting on March 25.
"I think everyone backpedaled a bit today," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It means we start next week with a much higher than usual level of uncertainty."

Despite the report, analysts said the Fed's next move on rates was an open question, noting Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan in recent comments focused on the need to quash future rather than current inflation risks.
But the severity of Thursday's sell-off, analysts said, meant the market had room to advance even without a clear green light on the interest rate front.
That sell-off was triggered by an unexpected surge in U.S. retail sales. While the rise suggested a surprisingly robust economy, analysts said the market's reaction was overblown.

"The data we saw yesterday didn't warrant a 160-point drop," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "But a lot of that may have been people anticipating a sloppy PPI and we certainly didn't get that."
With the Fed meeting still more than a week away, analysts said the market was unlikely to depart from its volatile ways anytime soon.

"Any sign of economic weakness will be taken as a temporary reason to rally," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates. "But it's all going to come down to what happens on the 25th."
Technology stocks were unable to hold early gains, and the Nasdaq composite index fell 0.31 point to 1,292.97, capping a loss of 18.83 for the week.
Tobacco stocks recouped some of Thursday's losses, with Philip Morris Cos Inc. rising three points to 129 and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. rising 5/8 to 33-7/8.
Among individual issues, Applied Magnetics Corp. fell 1-7/8 to 31-3/8 after abandoning its hostile attempt to acquire Read-Rite Corp. Shares in Read-Rite fell 3-1/8 to 26-5/8.

Employee Solutions Inc. tumbled 9-1/8 to 6-1/4, extending a slide that started Thursday, when the company said it would delay fourth quarter results. On Friday, it said its earnings for the period would be below analysts' estimates.
Fluor Corp. fell 6-3/4 to 57-3/4 after several Wall Street firms downgraded the shares.
Oracle Corp. jumped 4-7/8 to 41, a day after the company reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 3.61 points to 793.17 but lost 11.8 points for the week.
The American Stock Exchange index rose 2.45 to 600.47 but was off 1.59 for the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.83 to 417.70, but lost 6.13 for the week. The average price per share rose 19 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,580.93, up 27.803 or 0.37 percent. The index fell 106.188 on the week.
